越南箏源自中國古箏與瑟，潮州箏在阮朝時期傳入越南並本土化，與日本箏、伽倻琴、雅托: The đàn tranh comes from the Chinese guzheng and se; the Chaozhou zheng reached Vietnam in the Nguyễn dynasty and was localised there, and it shares an origin with the Japanese koto, the gayageum, the yatga and the Kazakh jetigen. It had fourteen strings in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth century, fifteen from the late fifteenth to the eighteenth century, and sixteen became standard in the nineteenth century, which is why it is also called the sixteen-string; that held until the late twentieth century. In the 1950s Nguyễn Vĩnh Bảo designed seventeen-, nineteen- and twenty-one-string versions, and the seventeen-string became the standard in Vietnam by the late 1980s, followed by twenty-two, twenty-four and twenty-five-string instruments. Early on it may have been used in court music and later passed into folk use; it can be played solo, in ensemble or as accompaniment.
越南箏琴身以木製為主，面板與底板多用泡桐木，側板、可移動弦柱、調音軸與小腳則為硬: The body of the đàn tranh is mostly wood: the soundboard and the back are usually paulownia, while the sides, the movable bridges, the tuning pegs and the small feet are hardwood; some sources also record that the bridges may be wood or bone covered with a layer of copper, and that the body may be lacquered or inlaid with mother-of-pearl. The sounding strings are steel, of different thicknesses. Players pluck with plectra of metal, plastic or turtle shell. The materials of the remaining parts are not recorded in the source.
越南箏的共鳴方式獨特，通過共鳴箱的特殊設計，使琴聲既具有古箏的柔和內斂，又比古箏: The đàn tranh resonates in its own way: the special design of the soundbox gives it the soft restraint of the Chinese guzheng while making it lighter and more agile than the guzheng. Its timbre is close to the elegance of the harp, yet it carries more of an Eastern spirit. Playing can produce vibrato, glissando and other effects, and the timbre is expressive. Against the deep, heavy Chinese guzheng it is more refined and elegant; against the Japanese koto it is livelier and brighter.
越南箏音色清亮透徹，具有獨特的東南亞韻味。其音質既不失絲竹樂器的溫潤感，又帶有金: The đàn tranh has a clear, transparent timbre with a distinctive Southeast Asian flavour. Its sound keeps the warmth of a silk-and-bamboo instrument while also having the bright sheen of metal strings. The range is wide, from a full low register to a crisp high one, clearly layered and richly expressive.
越南箏（Đàn tranh）屬弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號31: The đàn tranh (Đàn tranh) is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 312.22, from Vietnam in Southeast Asia. It can be played solo, take part in various instrumental ensembles, or accompany singing; it is also used for poetry recitation with music and for Vietnamese cải lương opera, and it sometimes enters the symphony orchestra or a chamber group. Its music is generally relaxed and cheerful, and new works extend the use of the fingers and of the voices. You can listen to Khúc Ngẫu Hứng trên Hò Đồng Tháp (1982), composed and played by Đặng Kim Hiền, on a 22-string đàn tranh.

The đàn tranh (Đàn tranh, also called đàn thập lục, the sixteen-string) is a plucked zither of Vietnam, Hornbostel–Sachs number 312.22. The body is a long soundbox, with steel strings, movable bridges and tuning pegs on the soundboard; the bridges are mostly inverted V-shaped and carry each string. Players usually pluck with plectra, the right hand sounding and the left hand pressing the strings to ornament. It can be played solo, in various instrumental ensembles, or to accompany singing, poetry recitation and cải lương opera, and it also appears in chamber groups or symphony orchestras.
